::: {.welcome}
Welcome. This is a vocabulary for talking about solar arrays on agricultural land: what one
does to a piece of ground, what it asks of the people who farm it, and what it might be made
to give back.

It is meant to be used rather than only read. The aim is that two people who have never met
can describe their sites to each other precisely, recognize the design problems they have in
common, and find the places where they genuinely disagree.
:::

## Why a shared language

A solar grazier, a township planner, a hydrologist, and a developer can stand on the same
eighty acres and describe it in four vocabularies that do not translate. Each of those
vocabularies is real: solar graziers, extension agents, agrivoltaic researchers,
community-solar developers, farmland-protection advocates, conservation biologists,
hydrologists, and county planners have each built genuine practice around their part of the
problem. They were built separately, though, so the parts do not compose — and until the words
line up, people cannot tell whether they actually disagree or are merely using terms
differently.

What is missing, then, is not another community. It is a translation layer between the ones
already at work: descriptive about how sites are built, and openly committed about what they
are for. The title says *restorative* on purpose. This document holds that ecological,
hydrological, and community function belong among the objectives of agrisolar design rather
than among its accidents — and it argues that position rather than assuming it. The
[preface](chapters/preface.qmd) sets out the commitment in full, along with who the document
is written for: the farmers, community decision-makers, and solar professionals who actually
make these decisions.

## The design language, in brief

Three structural devices carry the document — scale, sharing–sparing, and pressures — and two
further registers hang off them. All five are sketched here, so that a phrase met later
— *an A3 site at S2, carrying a hydrologic function* — reads as a sentence rather than a code.

### Where a project sits — the scale transect (§1) {#sec-intro-scale}

Scale settles what is physically, economically, and institutionally possible before design
begins, so it comes first. The [scale transect](chapters/1-the-scale-transect.qmd) is a single
gradient from the farmstead to the region, written **A1** through **A5**. It is a transect
rather than a set of size bins because several attributes move together along it: how a project
connects to the grid, who decides, what permitting it faces, and who manages the ground beneath
the panels.

::: {.zone-table}
| Zone | Indicative footprint | What changes at this size |
|---|---|---|
| **A1 — Farmstead** | under ~1 acre | One owner-operator, existing farm labor, behind the meter |
| **A2 — Field** | ~0.5–8 acres | Still the landowner's decision, perhaps one lease counterparty |
| **A3 — Parcel** | ~5–80 acres | Multi-party; ground-layer management becomes a contract |
| **A4 — Landscape** | ~60–400 acres | Developer-led; grazing and habitat become enterprises |
| **A5 — Regional** | ~300 to 10,000+ acres | Transmission, institutional capital, many jurisdictions |
:::

A sixth case sits at the origin: **A0**, arrays on buildings, which take no ground at all.
Capacity is given alongside acreage in [§1.2](chapters/1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones), but
where the two disagree, the land is the better guide to what the design problem will be.

![The scale transect. Interconnection posture, siting latitude, and restoration mode covary along one gradient — which is what makes it a transect rather than a set of size bins.](figures/fig_scale_transect.svg)

### What happens to production — the sharing–sparing axis (§2) {#sec-intro-sharing}

The second dimension, largely independent of the first. Does the array **share** the land with
agricultural production, **spare** land by taking ground out of it — or neither? The
[sharing–sparing axis](chapters/2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd) gives five positions, written
**S1** through **S5**:

::: {.position-table}
| Position | What it records |
|---|---|
| **S1 — Full sharing** | Production continues in the same ground, inside the footprint |
| **S2 — Functional sharing** | The ground layer is productive but subordinate — grazing, forage |
| **S3 — Coexistence** | *Neither.* Production stops on that ground, and the revenue sustains the farm enterprise that holds it |
| **S4 — Idled-land sparing** | The array takes ground already idle or marginal, sparing land that is not |
| **S5 — Impaired-land retirement** | Production ends on ground that was carrying a burden off-site |
:::

The centre of the axis is the honest one: most solar on farmland is neither sharing nor
sparing. **S3** exists to say so — and to mark the difference between a lease that keeps a
working farm solvent and a conversion that simply ends an operation. A position describes the
ground, never the goodness of the project.

### What pulls on a design — the design pressures (§3) {#sec-intro-pressures}

Every site is a settlement of forces that genuinely pull against one another.
[Eight of them](chapters/3-design-pressures.qmd) are named: generation yield, capital
discipline, operational simplicity, agricultural continuity, restorative ambition, social
license, offtake conformity, and decommissioning & reversibility. They are not axes — they have
direction, they conflict, and real people advocate for them. This is where the document takes
sides on purpose, and where it names the conflicts plainly rather than letting them surface as
vague friction.

### What the land is made to do — restorative functions (§4) {#sec-intro-functions}

Scale and position map where a project *sits*; they say nothing about restoration. So there is a
second register: five [restorative functions](chapters/4-restorative-functions.qmd) — hydrologic,
soil and carbon, biodiversity and habitat, microclimate, and community and economic — that are
reachable from many structural positions at once. They are a palette of capacities, not a
scorecard: no good project maximizes all of them, and some work against each other. Alongside
them sits the [SCALE footprint](chapters/4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale), which reads a
project's influence across four domains — Sustainable Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes,
Energy.

### How they settle — archetypes (§6) {#sec-intro-archetypes}

The design templates already in circulation are not the object of this lexicon. They are
[**archetypes**](chapters/6-archetypes.qmd) — recurring ways the pressures have been resolved at
a particular scale and sharing position, each carrying particular functions. Naming the forces
first is what lets a fifth, a sixth, and a twentieth archetype be described in the same language.

## Reading a site in the language

Put together, the pieces describe a real place in a few coordinates. Each site names its zone,
its position, the functions it carries, and which pressures it settled for — and which it gave
up, which the document calls the pressures it *yields*.

::: {.example}
**Solar prairie strips** are a **parcel-scale (A3)** form that retires the strip ground
(**S5**), planted where the field sheds its water, carrying **hydrologic** and
**biodiversity** functions. They are settled for **restorative ambition** and **social
license**, and yield a little **generation** to the prairie.
:::

::: {.example}
A **forty-kilowatt array over the barnyard**, shading the farm's own cows, is
**farmstead-scale (A1)** and **shares the ground (S1–S2)** with the animals already there.
It is settled for **agricultural continuity** and **operational simplicity**, and yields
**generation at scale** — the array is sized to the farm, not to the grid.
:::

Two projects that share almost nothing physically are now described in the same terms, which
is what makes it possible to say where they actually differ — and to compare either one with
whatever is being proposed down the road from you.

## How the document is organized

The three structural devices come first — [the scale
transect](chapters/1-the-scale-transect.qmd) (§1), [the sharing–sparing
axis](chapters/2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd) (§2), and [design
pressures](chapters/3-design-pressures.qmd) (§3). Then the [restorative
functions](chapters/4-restorative-functions.qmd) (§4) that give the title its structural home,
the [terminology](chapters/5-general-terminology.qmd) (§5) — every term the document defines,
grouped by register — and the [archetypes](chapters/6-archetypes.qmd) (§6) in which all of it
settles. The
[open issues](chapters/7-open-issues.qmd) (§7) close by showing the seams, and
[Sources](chapters/sources.qmd) records what has been verified and what has not.

It is written to be read in order. Nothing requires that of you, and the next section is for
readers who would rather not.

## Where to start

::: {.routes}
**If you have land in mind and want to know what is possible on it**, go to
[what appears at each scale](chapters/6-archetypes.qmd#sec-by-zone) — the forms that recur at
each size of project, from a barn roof to a regional complex, with what each one asks of the
ground.

**If you are weighing a specific proposal**, the
[design pressures](chapters/3-design-pressures.qmd) name the forces pulling on it and the
conflicts worth arguing about openly.

**If you are trying to pin down a term** someone has used, the
[alphabetical index](chapters/index-alphabetical.qmd) lists everything this document defines,
and the search box at the top of every page finds the rest.

**If you want the argument rather than the vocabulary**, start with the
[preface](chapters/preface.qmd) and read straight through.
:::

## Joining in

This is a working document, and it improves by being disagreed with. Corrections, counterexamples,
and proposed terms are welcome as issues or pull requests on
[GitHub](https://github.com/MSUHydrogeology/agrisolar_lexicon) — an archetype that recurs in your
region and is missing here, a term that lands badly with the people who have to use it, or a
citation you can trace further than we have.
